chunks: How a half/H-bridge works. The question: How does a half/H-Bridge work?
A half-bridge is two switches stacked between the supply and ground, with the output wire taken from the point between them.
Close the top switch and the output connects to the supply; close the bottom one and it connects to ground.
Flip between the two very fast and a motor sees an average voltage, so you can set its speed.
An H-bridge is two of these with the motor between them, so current can run either way.
Picture a tap that feeds a pipe from a high tank and a drain valve that dumps the pipe to the ground. Open the tap, then the drain, many times a second.
The water in the pipe settles to an in-between level set by how long the tap stays open.
The motor's coil acts like a heavy water wheel: it will not stop or start instantly, so it smooths the flicker.
Where it breaks: when the top switch opens, the coil's current keeps flowing, so the bottom switch must give it a path.
High side on. Current flows from V M through Q H and SW into the motor and down to ground. The winding stores energy: L di over dt equals V M-iR .
PWM: switching at a steady rate while changing how long each "on" lasts. Duty cycle ( D ): the fraction of each cycle the top switch is on. D equals 0.
25 means on 25% of the time. Inductor (winding): a coil that resists sudden changes in current, so its current cannot jump.
Freewheel path: the route the coil's current takes when the top switch opens, through the bottom switch or a diode built into it.
Dead time: a short gap with both switches off so they never conduct together.
Use a 12 volts supply and a motor on one half-bridge. Keep the top switch on for 25% of each cycle.
The output is 12 volts for a quarter of the time and 0 volts for the rest, so the average is 0. 25 times 12 equals 3 volts. That is the whole idea.
"A half-bridge connects the output to the supply or to ground, and PWM duty sets the average output.
The inductive motor current can't stop when the top switch opens, so it freewheels through the bottom FET or its body diode.
An H-bridge is two half-bridges with the motor in between: one leg high and the other low gives one direction, the opposite gives reverse, and PWM on one leg, or on both in anti-phase, sets speed.
Dead time keeps both FETs in a leg from conducting together."
